In [[geometry]], '''Coxeter notation''' (also '''Coxeter symbol''') is a system of classifying [[symmetry group]]s, describing the angles between fundamental reflections of a [[Coxeter group]] in a bracketed notation expressing the structure of a [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]], with modifiers to indicate certain subgroups.  The notation is named after [[H. S. M. Coxeter]], and has been more comprehensively defined by [[Norman Johnson (mathematician)|Norman Johnson]].

== Reflectional groups==
{{Further|Point group}}

For [[Coxeter group]]s, defined by pure reflections, there is a direct correspondence between the bracket notation and [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]]. The numbers in the bracket notation represent the mirror reflection orders in the branches of the Coxeter diagram. It uses the same simplification, suppressing 2s between orthogonal mirrors.

The Coxeter notation is simplified with exponents to represent the number of branches in a row for linear diagram. So the ''A''<sub>''n''</sub> group is represented by [3<sup>''n''−1</sup>], to imply ''n'' nodes connected by ''n−1'' order-3 branches. Example ''A''<sub>2</sub> = [3,3] = [3<sup>2</sup>] or [3<sup>1,1</sup>] represents diagrams {{CDD|node|3|node|3|node}} or {{CDD|node|split1|nodes}}.

Coxeter initially represented bifurcating diagrams with vertical positioning of numbers, but later abbreviated with an exponent notation, like [...,3<sup>p,q</sup>] or [3<sup>p,q,r</sup>], starting with [3<sup>1,1,1</sup>] or [3,3<sup>1,1</sup>] = {{CDD|node|splitsplit1|branch3|node}} or  {{CDD|node|3|node|split1|nodes}} as D<sub>4</sub>. Coxeter allowed for zeros as special cases to fit the ''A''<sub>''n''</sub> family, like ''A''<sub>3</sub> = [3,3,3,3] = [3<sup>4,0,0</sup>] = [3<sup>4,0</sup>] = [3<sup>3,1</sup>] = [3<sup>2,2</sup>], like {{CDD|node|3|node|3|node|3|node|3|node}} = {{CDD|node|split1|nodes|3a|nodea|3a|nodea}} = {{CDD|node|split1|nodes|3ab|nodes}}.

Coxeter groups formed by cyclic diagrams are represented by parentheses inside of brackets, like [(p,q,r)] = {{CDD|pqr}} for the [[triangle group]] (p q r). If the branch orders are equal, they can be grouped as an exponent as the length the cycle in brackets, like [(3,3,3,3)] = [3<sup>[4]</sup>], representing Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node|split1|nodes|split2|node}} or {{CDD|branch|3ab|branch}}. {{CDD|node|3|node|split1|branch}} can be represented as [3,(3,3,3)] or [3,3<sup>[3]</sup>].

More complicated looping diagrams can also be expressed with care. The [[Coxeter–Dynkin diagram#Ranks 4.E2.80.9310|paracompact Coxeter group]] {{CDD|node|split1|branch|split2|node}} can be represented by Coxeter notation [(3,3,(3),3,3)], with nested/overlapping parentheses showing two adjacent [(3,3,3)] loops, and is also represented more compactly as [3<sup>[&nbsp;]×[&nbsp;]</sup>], representing the [[rhombus|rhombic symmetry]] of the Coxeter diagram. The paracompact complete graph diagram {{CDD|tet}} or  {{CDD|branch|splitcross|branch}}, is represented as [3<sup>[3,3]</sup>] with the superscript [3,3] as the symmetry of its [[regular tetrahedron]] Coxeter diagram.

For the affine and hyperbolic groups, the subscript is one less than the number of nodes in each case, since each of these groups was obtained by adding a node to a finite group's diagram.

== Unconnected groups ==

The Coxeter diagram usually leaves order-2 branches undrawn, but the bracket notation includes an explicit '''2''' to connect the subgraphs. So the Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node|3|node|2|node|3|node}} = ''A''<sub>2</sub>×''A''<sub>2</sub> = 2''A''<sub>2</sub> can be represented by [3]×[3] = [3]<sup>2</sup> = [3,2,3]. Sometimes explicit 2-branches may be included either with a 2 label, or with a line with a gap: {{CDD|node|3|node|2x|node|3|node}} or {{CDD|node|3|node|3|2|3|node|3|node}}, as an identical presentation as [3,2,3].

== Rank and dimension==
Coxeter point group rank is equal to the number of nodes which is also equal to the dimension. A single mirror exists in 1-dimension, [&nbsp;], {{CDD|node}}, while in 2-dimensions [1], {{CDD|node|2|node_h2}} or [&nbsp;]×[&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup>. The '''1''' is a place-holder, not an actual branch order, but a marker for an orthogonal inactive mirror. The notation [''n'',1], represents a rank 3 group, as [''n'']×[&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup> or {{CDD|node|n||node||2|node_h2}}. Similarly, [1,1] as [&nbsp;]×[&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup>×[&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup> or {{CDD|node|2|node_h2|2|node_h2}} order 2 and [1,1]<sup>+</sup> as [&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup>×[&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup>×[&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup> or {{CDD|node_h2|2|node_h2|2|node_h2}}, order 1!

== Subgroups ==
Coxeter's notation represents rotational/translational symmetry by adding a '''<sup>+</sup>''' superscript operator outside the brackets, [X]<sup>+</sup> which cuts the order of the group [X] in half, thus an index 2 subgroup. This operator implies an even number of operators must be applied, replacing reflections with rotations (or translations). When applied to a Coxeter group, this is called a '''direct subgroup''' because what remains are only direct isometries without reflective symmetry.

The '''<sup>+</sup>''' operators can also be applied inside of the brackets, like [X,Y<sup>+</sup>] or [X,(Y,Z)<sup>+</sup>], and creates '''"semidirect" subgroups''' that may include both reflective and nonreflective generators. Semidirect subgroups can only apply to Coxeter group subgroups that have even order branches adjacent to it. Elements by parentheses inside of a Coxeter group can be give a '''<sup>+</sup>''' superscript operator, having the effect of dividing adjacent ordered branches into half order, thus is usually only applied with even numbers. For example, [4,3<sup>+</sup>] and [4,(3,3)<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node|4|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}).

If applied with adjacent odd branch, it doesn't create a subgroup of index 2, but instead creates overlapping fundamental domains, like [5,1<sup>+</sup>] = [5/2], which can define doubly wrapped polygons like a [[pentagram]], {5/2}, and [5,3<sup>+</sup>] relates to [[Schwarz triangle]] [5/2,3], [[polytope density|density]] 2.

Groups without neighboring '''<sup>+</sup>''' elements can be seen in ringed nodes Coxeter-Dynkin diagram for [[uniform polytope]]s and honeycomb are related to ''hole'' nodes around the '''<sup>+</sup>''' elements, empty circles with the alternated nodes removed. So the [[snub cube]], {{CDD|node_h|4|node_h|3|node_h}} has symmetry [4,3]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}), and the [[snub tetrahedron]], {{CDD|node|4|node_h|3|node_h}} has symmetry [4,3<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}), and a [[demicube]], h{4,3} = {3,3} ({{CDD|node_h|4|node|3|node}} or {{CDD|nodes_10ru|split2|node}} = {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3|node}}) has symmetry [1<sup>+</sup>,4,3] = [3,3] ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node|3|node}} or {{CDD|node_h0|4|node|3|node}} = {{CDD|nodes|split2|node}} = {{CDD|node|3|node|3|node}}).

Note: [[Pyritohedral symmetry]] {{CDD|node|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}} can be written as {{CDD|node|4|2c|node_h2|3|node_h2}}, separating the graph with gaps for clarity, with the generators {0,1,2} from the Coxeter group {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|3|node_n2}}, producing pyritohedral generators {0,12}, a reflection and 3-fold rotation. And chiral tetrahedral symmetry can be written as  {{CDD|node_h0|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}} or  {{CDD|node_h2|2c|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}, [1<sup>+</sup>,4,3<sup>+</sup>] = [3,3]<sup>+</sup>, with generators {12,0120}.

Johnson extends the '''<sup>+</sup>''' operator to work with a placeholder 1<sup>+</sup> nodes, which removes mirrors, doubling the size of the fundamental domain and cuts the group order in half.<ref name="subgroups2">Johnson (2018), 11.6 ''Subgroups and extensions'', p 255, halving subgroups</ref> In general this operation only applies to individual mirrors bounded by even-order branches. The '''1''' represents a mirror so [2p] can be seen as [2p,<span style="color:#00ff00;">1</span>], [<span style="color:red;">1</span>,2p], or [<span style="color:red;">1</span>,2p,<span style="color:#00ff00;">1</span>], like diagram {{CDD|node|2x|p|node}} or {{CDD|node_c1|2x|p|node_c3}}, with 2 mirrors related by an order-2p dihedral angle. The effect of a mirror removal is to duplicate connecting nodes, which can be seen in the Coxeter diagrams: {{CDD|node_h0|2x|p|node_c3}} = {{CDD|labelp|branch_c3}}, or in bracket notation:[1<sup>+</sup>,2p, <span style="color:#00ff00;">1</span>] = [<span style="color:#00ff00;">1</span>,p,<span style="color:#00ff00;">1</span>] = [p].

Each of these mirrors can be removed so h[2p] = [1<sup>+</sup>,2p,1] = [1,2p,1<sup>+</sup>] = [p], a reflective subgroup index 2. This can be shown in a Coxeter diagram by adding a <sup>+</sup> symbol above the node: {{CDD|node_h0|2x|p|node}} = {{CDD|node|2x|p|node_h0}} = {{CDD|labelp|branch}}.

If both mirrors are removed, a quarter subgroup is generated, with the branch order becoming a gyration point of half the order: 
:q[2p] = [1<sup>+</sup>,2p,1<sup>+</sup>] = [p]<sup>+</sup>, a rotational subgroup of index 4. {{CDD|node_h2|2c|2x|p|2c|node_h2}} = {{CDD|node_h0|2x|p|node_h0}} = {{CDD|node_h0|2x|p|node_h2}} = {{CDD|node_h2|2x|p|node_h0}} =  {{CDD|labelp|branch_h2h2}}.

For example, (with p=2): [4,1<sup>+</sup>] = [1<sup>+</sup>,4] = [2] = [&nbsp;]×[&nbsp;], order 4. [1<sup>+</sup>,4,1<sup>+</sup>] = [2]<sup>+</sup>, order 2.

The opposite to halving is doubling<ref name="subgroups"/> which adds a mirror, bisecting a fundamental domain, and doubling the group order.
: {{Brackets|p}} = [2p]

Halving operations apply for higher rank groups, like [[tetrahedral symmetry]] is a half group of [[octahedral group]]: h[4,3] = [1<sup>+</sup>,4,3] = [3,3], removing half the mirrors at the 4-branch. The effect of a mirror removal is to duplicate all connecting nodes, which can be seen in the Coxeter diagrams: {{CDD|node_h0|2x|p|node_c1|3|node_c2}} = {{CDD|labelp|branch_c1|split2|node_c2}}, h[2p,3] = [1<sup>+</sup>,2p,3] = [(p,3,3)].

If nodes are indexed, half subgroups can be labeled with new mirrors as composites. Like {{CDD|node_n0|2x|p|node_n1}}, generators {0,1} has subgroup {{CDD|node_h0|2x|p|node_n1}} = {{CDD|2_n0|node_n1|3_n0|p|node_n1}}, generators {1,010}, where mirror 0 is removed, and replaced by a copy of mirror 1 reflected across mirror 0. Also given {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|3|node_n2}}, generators {0,1,2}, it has half group {{CDD|node_h0|4|node_n1|3|node_n2}} = {{CDD|node_n1|3|node_n2|3|3_n0|node_n1|2_n0}}, generators {1,2,010}.

Doubling by adding a mirror also applies in reversing the halving operation: {{Brackets|3,3}} = [4,3], or more generally {{Brackets|(q,q,p)}} = [2p,q].
{| class=wikitable
![[Tetrahedral symmetry]]
![[Octahedral symmetry]]
|- align=center
|[[File:Sphere symmetry group td.svg|150px]]<br>T<sub>d</sub>, [3,3] = [1<sup>+</sup>,4,3]<br>{{CDD|node_c1|3|node_c1|3|node_c1}} = {{CDD|nodeab_c1|split2|node_c1}} = {{CDD|node_h0|4|node_c1|3|node_c1}}<br>(Order 24)
|[[File:Sphere symmetry group oh.svg|150px]]<br>O<sub>h</sub>, [4,3] = {{Brackets|3,3}}<br>{{CDD|node_c2|4|node_c1|3|node_c1}}<br>(Order 48)
|}

=== Radical subgroups ===
[[File:43-radial subgroups.svg|thumb|A radical subgroup is similar to an alternation, but removes the rotational generators.]]
Johnson also added an [[asterisk]] or star '''*''' operator for "radical" subgroups,<ref>Johnson (2018), 11.6 ''Subgroups and extensions'', p 259, radical subgroup</ref> that acts similar to the <sup>+</sup> operator, but removes rotational symmetry. The index of the radical subgroup is the order of the removed element.  For example, [4,3*] ≅ [2,2]. The removed [3] subgroup is order 6 so [2,2] is an index 6 subgroup of [4,3].

The radical subgroups represent the inverse operation to an [[#Extended symmetry|extended symmetry]] operation. For example, [4,3*] ≅ [2,2], and in reverse [2,2] can be extended as [3[2,2]] ≅ [4,3]. The subgroups can be expressed as a Coxeter diagram: {{CDD|node_c1|4|node|3s|node}} or {{CDD|node_c1|4|node_x|3|node_x}} ≅ {{CDD|nodeab_c1|2|node_c1}}. The removed node (mirror) causes adjacent mirror virtual mirrors to become real mirrors.

If [4,3] has generators {0,1,2}, [4,3<sup>+</sup>], index 2, has generators {0,12}; [1<sup>+</sup>,4,3] ≅ [3,3], index 2 has generators {010,1,2}; while radical subgroup [4,3*] ≅ [2,2], index 6, has generators {01210, 2, (012)<sup>3</sup>}; and finally [1<sup>+</sup>,4,3*], index 12 has generators {0(12)<sup>2</sup>0, (012)<sup>2</sup>01}.

{{Clear}}

=== Trionic subgroups ===
[[File:Trionic subgroups hexagonal symmetry.png|120px|thumb|left|Rank 2 example, [6] trionic subgroups with 3 colors of mirror lines]]
[[File:432 trionic subgroups.png|thumb|Example on octahedral symmetry: [4,3<sup>⅄</sup>] = [2,4].]]
[[File:Trionic subgroups hexagonal.png|thumb|Example trionic subgroup on hexagonal symmetry [6,3] maps onto a larger [6,3] symmetry.]]
[[File:Trionic Coxeter groups rank 3.png|120px|thumb|left|Rank 3]]
[[File:Hyperbolic 832 trionic subgroup 842.png|thumb|Example trionic subgroups on octagonal symmetry [8,3] maps onto larger [4,8] symmetries.]]
[[File:Trionic subgroups rank 4b.png|120px|thumb|left|Rank 4]]
A '''trionic subgroup''' is an index 3 subgroup. Johnson defines a ''trionic subgroup'' with operator ⅄, index 3. For rank 2 Coxeter groups, [3], the trionic subgroup, [3<sup>⅄</sup>] is [ ], a single mirror. And for [3''p''], the trionic subgroup is [3''p'']<sup>⅄</sup> ≅ [''p'']. Given {{CDD|node_n0|3x|p|node_n1}}, with generators {0,1}, has 3 trionic subgroups. They can be differentiated by putting the ⅄ symbol next to the mirror generator to be removed, or on a branch for both: [3''p'',1<sup>⅄</sup>] = {{CDD|node_n0|3x|p|node_trionic}} = {{CDD|node_n0|p|3_n1|3_n0|node_n1|2_n0|2_n1}},  {{CDD|node_trionic|3x|p|node_n1}} = {{CDD|2_n0|2_n1|node_n0|3_n1|3_n0|p|node_n1}}, and [3''p''<sup>⅄</sup>] = {{CDD|node_n0|3x|3trionic|p|node_n1}} = {{CDD|2_n0|node_n1|3_n0|p|3_n1|node_n0|2_n1}} with generators {0,10101}, {01010,1}, or {101,010}.

[[#Trionic subgroups of tetrahedral symmetry|Trionic subgroups of tetrahedral symmetry]]: [3,3]<sup>⅄</sup> ≅ [2<sup>+</sup>,4], relating the symmetry of the [[regular tetrahedron]] and [[tetragonal disphenoid]].

For rank 3 Coxeter groups, [''p'',3], there is a trionic subgroup [''p'',3<sup>⅄</sup>] ≅ [''p''/2,''p''], or {{CDD|node_n0|2x|p|node_n1|3trionic|node_n2}} = {{CDD|2_n2|2_n1|node_n0|3_n1|3_n2|p|node_n0|2x|p|node_n1}}. For example, the finite group [4,3<sup>⅄</sup>] ≅ [2,4], and Euclidean group [6,3<sup>⅄</sup>] ≅ [3,6], and hyperbolic group [8,3<sup>⅄</sup>] ≅ [4,8].

An odd-order adjacent branch, ''p'', will not lower the group order, but create overlapping fundamental domains. The group order stays the same, while the [[density (polytope)|density]] increases. For example, the [[icosahedral symmetry]], [5,3], of the regular polyhedra [[icosahedron]] becomes [5/2,5], the symmetry of 2 regular star polyhedra. It also relates the hyperbolic tilings {p,3}, and [[List of regular polytopes and compounds#Hyperbolic star-tilings|star hyperbolic tilings]] {p/2,p}

For rank 4, [''q'',2''p'',3<sup>⅄</sup>] = [2''p'',((p,q,q))], {{CDD|node|q|node|2x|p|node|3trionic|node}} = {{CDD|labelq|branch|split2-pq|node|2x|p|node}}.

For example, [3,4,3<sup>⅄</sup>] = [4,3,3], or {{CDD|node_n0|3|node_n1|4|node_n2|3trionic|node_n3}} = {{CDD|2_n3|2_n2|node_n1|3_n2|3_n3|3|node_n0|3|node_n1|4|node_n2}}, generators {0,1,2,3} in [3,4,3] with the trionic subgroup [4,3,3] generators {0,1,2,32123}. For hyperbolic groups, [3,6,3<sup>⅄</sup>] = [6,3<sup>[3]</sup>], and [4,4,3<sup>⅄</sup>] = [4,4,4].

{{Clear}}

==== Trionic subgroups of tetrahedral symmetry====
[[File:Trionic_subgroups_of_tetrahedral_symmetry_stereographic_projection.png|thumb|left|[3,3]<sup>⅄</sup> ≅ [2<sup>+</sup>,4] as one of 3 sets of 2 orthogonal mirrors in [[stereographic projection]]. The red, green, and blue represent 3 sets of mirrors, and the gray lines are removed mirrors, leaving 2-fold gyrations (purple diamonds).]]
[[File:33-trionic subgroups.png|thumb|Trionic relations of [3,3]]]
Johnson identified two specific '''trionic subgroups'''<ref>Johnson (2018), 11.6 ''Subgroups and extensions'', p 258, trionic subgroups</ref> of [3,3], first an index 3 subgroup [3,3]<sup>⅄</sup> ≅ [2<sup>+</sup>,4], with [3,3] ({{CDD|node_n0|3|node_n1|3|node_n2}} = {{CDD|node|split1|nodes}} = {{CDD|node|split1|branch|label2}}) generators {0,1,2}. It can also be written as [(3,3,2<sup>⅄</sup>)] ({{CDD|node|split1|2c|branch_h2h2|label2}}) as a reminder of its generators {02,1}. This symmetry reduction is the relationship between the regular [[tetrahedron]] and the [[tetragonal disphenoid]], represent a stretching of a tetrahedron perpendicular to two opposite edges.

Secondly he identifies a related index 6 subgroup [3,3]<sup>Δ</sup> or [(3,3,2<sup>⅄</sup>)]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|split1|2c|branch_h2h2|label2}}), index 3 from [3,3]<sup>+</sup> ≅ [2,2]<sup>+</sup>, with generators {02,1021}, from [3,3] and its generators {0,1,2}.

These subgroups also apply within larger Coxeter groups with [3,3] subgroup with neighboring branches all even order.
[[File:334 trionic subgroups2.png|thumb|Trionic subgroup relations of [3,3,4]]]
For example, [(3,3)<sup>+</sup>,4], [(3,3)<sup>⅄</sup>,4], and [(3,3)<sup>Δ</sup>,4] are subgroups of [3,3,4], index 2, 3 and 6 respectively. The generators of [(3,3)<sup>⅄</sup>,4] ≅ {{Brackets|4,2,4}} ≅ [8,2<sup>+</sup>,8], order 128, are {02,1,3} from [3,3,4] generators {0,1,2,3}. And [(3,3)<sup>Δ</sup>,4] ≅ {{Brackets|4,2<sup>+</sup>,4}}, order 64, has generators {02,1021,3}. As well, [3<sup>⅄</sup>,4,3<sup>⅄</sup>] ≅ [(3,3)<sup>⅄</sup>,4].

Also related [3<sup>1,1,1</sup>] = [3,3,4,1<sup>+</sup>] has trionic subgroups: [3<sup>1,1,1</sup>]<sup>⅄</sup> = [(3,3)<sup>⅄</sup>,4,1<sup>+</sup>], order 64, and 1=[3<sup>1,1,1</sup>]<sup>Δ</sup> = [(3,3)<sup>Δ</sup>,4,1<sup>+</sup>] ≅ [[4,2<sup>+</sup>,4]]<sup>+</sup>, order 32.

{{Clear}}

=== Central inversion===
[[File:Point Reflection.png|thumb|A 2D central inversion is a 180 degree rotation, [2]<sup>+</sup>]]
A [[central inversion]], order 2, is operationally differently by dimension. The group [&nbsp;]<sup>''n''</sup> = [2<sup>''n''−1</sup>] represents ''n'' orthogonal mirrors in n-dimensional space, or an [[n-flat]] subspace of a higher dimensional space. The mirrors of the group [2<sup>''n''−1</sup>] are numbered {{tmath|0 \dots n-1}}. The order of the mirrors doesn't matter in the case of an inversion. The matrix of a central inversion is {{tmath|-I}}, the Identity matrix with negative one on the diagonal.

From that basis, the central inversion has a generator as the product of all the orthogonal mirrors. In Coxeter notation this inversion group is expressed by adding an alternation <sup>+</sup> to each 2 branch. The alternation symmetry is marked on Coxeter diagram nodes as open nodes.

A [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]] can be marked up with explicit 2 branches defining a linear sequence of mirrors, open-nodes, and shared double-open nodes to show the chaining of the reflection generators.

For example, [2<sup>+</sup>,2] and [2,2<sup>+</sup>] are subgroups index 2 of [2,2], {{CDD|node|2|node|2|node}}, and are represented as {{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h2|2|node}} (or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2|2|node}}) and {{CDD|node|2|node_h2|2x|node_h2}} (or {{CDD|node|2|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2}}) with generators {01,2} and {0,12} respectively. Their common subgroup index 4 is [2<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>], and is represented by {{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h4|2x|node_h2}} (or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h4|3|2c|3|node_h2}}), with the double-open {{CDD|node_h4}} marking a shared node in the two alternations, and a single [[rotoreflection]] generator {012}.

=== Rotations and rotary reflections ===
Rotations and [[rotary reflection]]s are constructed by a single single-generator product of all the reflections of a prismatic group, [2''p'']×[2''q'']×... where [[Greatest common divisor|gcd]](''p'',''q'',...)=1, they are isomorphic to the abstract [[cyclic group]] Z<sub>n</sub>, of order ''n''=2''pq''.

The 4-dimensional double rotations, [2''p''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,2''q''<sup>+</sup>] (with [[Greatest common divisor|gcd]](''p'',''q'')=1), which include a central group, and are expressed by Conway as ±[C<sub>''p''</sub>×C<sub>''q''</sub>],<ref>Conway, 2003, p.46, Table 4.2 Chiral groups II</ref> order 2''pq''. From Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_n0|2x|p|node_n1|2|node_n2|2x|q|node_n3}}, generators {0,1,2,3}, requires two generator for [2''p''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,2''q''<sup>+</sup>], {{CDD|node_h2|2x|p|node_h4|2x|node_h4|2x|q|node_h2}} as {0123,0132}. Half groups, [2''p''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,2''q''<sup>+</sup>]<sup>+</sup>, or cyclic graph, [(2''p''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,2''q''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>)], {{CDD|3|node_h4|2x|p|node_h4|2x|node_h4|2x|q|node_h4|2x}} expressed by Conway is [C<sub>''p''</sub>×C<sub>''q''</sub>], order ''pq'', with one generator, like {0123}.

If there is a common factor ''f'', the double rotation can be written as {{frac|1|''f''}}[2''pf''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,2''qf''<sup>+</sup>] (with [[Greatest common divisor|gcd]](''p'',''q'')=1), generators {0123,0132}, order 2''pqf''. For example, ''p''=''q''=1, ''f''=2, {{frac|1|2}}[4<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,4<sup>+</sup>] is order 4. And {{frac|1|''f''}}[2''pf''<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,2''qf''<sup>+</sup>]<sup>+</sup>, generator {0123}, is order ''pqf''. For example, {{frac|1|2}}[4<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>,4<sup>+</sup>]<sup>+</sup> is order 2, a [[central inversion]].

In general a ''n''-rotation group, [2''p''<sub>1</sub><sup>+</sup>,2,2''p''<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>,2,...,''p''<sub>''n''</sub><sup>+</sup>] may require up to ''n'' generators if gcd(''p''<sub>1</sub>,..,''p''<sub>''n''</sub>)>1, as a product of all mirrors, and then swapping sequential pairs. The half group, [2''p''<sub>1</sub><sup>+</sup>,2,2''p''<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>,2,...,''p''<sub>''n''</sub><sup>+</sup>]<sup>+</sup> has generators squared. ''n''-rotary reflections are similar.

=== Commutator subgroups ===
[[File:Subgroups of 442.png|thumb|360px|[[Hasse diagram]] subgroups of [4,4], down to its commutator subgroup, index 8]]
Simple groups with only odd-order branch elements have only a single rotational/translational subgroup of order 2, which is also the [[commutator subgroup]], examples [3,3]<sup>+</sup>, [3,5]<sup>+</sup>, [3,3,3]<sup>+</sup>, [3,3,5]<sup>+</sup>. For other Coxeter groups with even-order branches, the commutator subgroup has index 2<sup>''c''</sup>, where c is the number of disconnected subgraphs when all the even-order branches are removed.<ref>Coxeter and Moser, 1980, Sec 9.5 Commutator subgroup, p. 124–126</ref>

For example, [4,4] has three independent nodes in the Coxeter diagram when the '''4'''s are removed, so its commutator subgroup is index 2<sup>3</sup>, and can have different representations, all with three '''<sup>+</sup>''' operators: [4<sup>+</sup>,4<sup>+</sup>]<sup>+</sup>, [1<sup>+</sup>,4,1<sup>+</sup>,4,1<sup>+</sup>], [1<sup>+</sup>,4,4,1<sup>+</sup>]<sup>+</sup>, or [(4<sup>+</sup>,4<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>)]. A general notation can be used with +''c'' as a group exponent, like [4,4]<sup>+3</sup>.

=== Example subgroups ===

==== Rank 2 example subgroups ====
[[Dihedral symmetry]] groups with even-orders have a number of subgroups. This example shows two generator mirrors of [4] in red and green, and looks at all subgroups by halving, rank-reduction, and their direct subgroups. The group [4], {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1}} has two mirror generators 0, and 1. Each generate two virtual mirrors 101 and 010 by reflection across the other.

==== Rank 3 Euclidean example subgroups ====
The [4,4] group has 15 small index subgroups. This table shows them all, with a yellow fundamental domain for pure reflective groups, and alternating white and blue domains which are paired up to make rotational domains. Cyan, red, and green mirror lines correspond to the same colored nodes in the Coxeter diagram. Subgroup generators can be expressed as products of the original 3 mirrors of the fundamental domain, {0,1,2}, corresponding to the 3 nodes of the Coxeter diagram, {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|4|node_n2}}. A product of two intersecting reflection lines makes a rotation, like {012}, {12}, or {02}. Removing a mirror causes two copies of neighboring mirrors, across the removed mirror, like {010}, and {212}. Two rotations in series cut the rotation order in half, like {0101} or {(01)<sup>2</sup>}, {1212} or {(02)<sup>2</sup>}. A product of all three mirrors creates a [[transreflection]], like {012} or {120}.

|[6*,4]<sup>+</sup><br>{{CDD|node|6|3s|node|4|node_h2}}<br>(222222)

=== Parabolic subgroups===
A [[parabolic subgroup of a reflection group|parabolic subgroup]] of a Coxeter group can be identified by removing one or more generator mirrors represented with a Coxeter diagram. For example, the octahedral group {{CDD|node_n1|4|node_n2|3|node_n3}} has parabolic subgroups {{CDD|node_n1|4|node_n2}}, {{CDD|node_n1|2|node_n3}}, {{CDD|node_n2|3|node_n3}}, {{CDD|node_n1}}, {{CDD|node_n2}}, {{CDD|node_n3}}. In bracket notation [4,3] has parabolic subgroups [4],[2],[3], and a single mirror []. The order of the subgroup is known, and always an integer divisor group order, or index. Parabolic subgroups can also be written with x nodes, like {{CDD|node_n1|4|node_n2|3|node_n3}}=[4,3] subgroup by removing second mirror: {{CDD|node_n1|4|node_x|3|node_n3}} or {{CDD|node_n1|2|node_x|2|node_n3}} = {{CDD|node_n1|2|node_n3}} = [4,1<sup>×</sup>,3] = [2].

=== Petrie subgroup===
A ''petrie subgroup'' of an irreducible coxeter group can be created by the product of all of the generators. It can be seen in the skew regular [[petrie polygon]] of a [[regular polytope]]. The order of the new group is called the [[Coxeter number]] of the original Coxeter group. The ''Coxeter number'' of a Coxeter group is 2''m''/''n'', where ''n'' is the rank, and ''m'' is the number of reflections. A petrie subgroup can be written with a {{pi}} superscript. For example, [3,3]<sup>{{pi}}</sup> is the petrie subgroup of a tetrahedral group, cyclic group order 4, generated by a [[rotoreflection]]. A rank 4 Coxeter group will have a [[double rotation]] generator, like [4,3,3]<sup>{{pi}}</sup> is order 8.

== Extended symmetry==
{| class=wikitable align=right width=100
|{{A2 honeycombs}}
|-
|In the Euclidean plane, the <math>{\tilde{A}}_2</math>, [3<sup>[3]</sup>] Coxeter group can be extended in two ways into the <math>{\tilde{G}}_2</math>, [6,3] Coxeter group and relates uniform tilings as ringed diagrams.
|}

{{See also|Goursat tetrahedron#Extended symmetry}}

Coxeter's notation includes double square bracket notation, {{Brackets|X}} to express [[automorphism|automorphic]] symmetry within a Coxeter diagram. Johnson added alternative doubling by angled-bracket <[X]>. Johnson also added a prefix symmetry modifier [Y[X]], where Y can either represent symmetry of the Coxeter diagram of [X], or symmetry of the fundamental domain of [X].

For example, in 3D these equivalent [[rectangle]] and [[Rhombus|rhombic]] geometry diagrams of <math>{\tilde{A}}_3</math>: {{CDD|branch|3ab|3ab|branch}} and {{CDD|node|split1|nodes|split2|node}}, the first doubled with square brackets, {{Brackets|3<sup>{{Bracket|4}}</sup>}} or twice doubled as [2[3<sup>[4]</sup>]], with [2], order 4 higher symmetry. To differentiate the second, angled brackets are used for doubling, <[3<sup>[4]</sup>]> and twice doubled as <2[3<sup>[4]</sup>]>, also with a different [2], order 4 symmetry. Finally a full symmetry where all 4 nodes are equivalent can be represented by [4[3<sup>[4]</sup>]], with the order 8, [4] symmetry of the [[Square (geometry)|square]]. But by considering the [[tetragonal disphenoid]] fundamental domain the [4] extended symmetry of the square graph can be marked more explicitly as [(2<sup>+</sup>,4)[3<sup>[4]</sup>]] or [2<sup>+</sup>,4[3<sup>[4]</sup>]].

Further symmetry exists in the cyclic <math>{\tilde{A}}_n</math> and branching <math>D_3</math>, <math>{\tilde{E}}_6</math>, and <math>{\tilde{D}}_4</math> diagrams. <math>{\tilde{A}}_n</math> has order 2''n'' symmetry of a regular ''n''-gon, {''n''}, and is represented by [''n''[3<sup>[''n'']</sup>]]. <math>D_3</math> and <math>{\tilde{E}}_6</math> are represented by [3[3<sup>1,1,1</sup>]] = [3,4,3] and [3[3<sup>2,2,2</sup>]] respectively while <math>{\tilde{D}}_4</math> by [(3,3)[3<sup>1,1,1,1</sup>]] = [3,3,4,3], with the diagram containing the order 24 symmetry of the regular [[tetrahedron]], {3,3}. The paracompact hyperbolic group <math>{\bar{L}}_5</math> = [3<sup>1,1,1,1,1</sup>], {{CDD|node|branch3|splitsplit2|node|split1|nodes}}, contains the symmetry of a [[5-cell]], {3,3,3}, and thus is represented by [(3,3,3)[3<sup>1,1,1,1,1</sup>]] = [3,4,3,3,3].

An [[asterisk]] * superscript is effectively an inverse operation, creating ''radical subgroups'' removing connected of odd-ordered mirrors.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1016/S0024-3795(99)00107-X| title=Quaternionic modular groups| journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications| volume=295| issue=1–3| pages=159–189| year=1999| last1=Johnson| first1=Norman W.| last2=Weiss| first2=Asia Ivić| doi-access=free}}</ref>

Looking at generators, the double symmetry is seen as adding a new operator that maps symmetric positions in the Coxeter diagram, making some original generators redundant. For 3D [[space group]]s, and 4D point groups, Coxeter defines an index two subgroup of {{Brackets|X}}, {{Brackets|X|<sup>+</sup>}}, which he defines as the product of the original generators of [X] by the doubling generator. This looks similar to {{Brackets|X}}<sup>+</sup>, which is the chiral subgroup of {{Brackets|X}}. So for example the 3D space groups {{Brackets|4,3,4}}<sup>+</sup> (I432, 211) and {{Brackets|4,3,4|<sup>+</sup>}} (Pm{{overline|3}}n, 
223) are distinct subgroups of {{Brackets|4,3,4}} (Im{{overline|3}}m, 229).

== Rank one groups==
{{Further|One-dimensional symmetry group}}
In one dimension, the ''bilateral group'' [&nbsp;] represents a single mirror symmetry, abstract ''Dih''<sub>1</sub> or ''Z''<sub>2</sub>, symmetry [[Order (group theory)|order]] 2. It is represented as a [[Coxeter–Dynkin diagram]] with a single node, {{CDD|node}}. The ''[[trivial group|identity group]]'' is the direct subgroup [&nbsp;]<sup>+</sup>, Z<sub>1</sub>, symmetry order 1. The '''+''' superscript simply implies that alternate mirror reflections are ignored, leaving the identity group in this simplest case. Coxeter used a single open node to represent an alternation, {{CDD|node_h2}}.

== Rank two groups==
{{Further|Point groups in two dimensions}}
[[File:Regular hexagon symmetries2.png|400px|thumb|A regular [[hexagon]], with markings on edges and vertices has 8 symmetries: [6], [3], [2], [1], [6]<sup>+</sup>, [3]<sup>+</sup>, [2]<sup>+</sup>, [1]<sup>+</sup>, with [3] and [1] existing in two forms, depending whether the mirrors are on the edges or vertices.]]
In two dimensions, the ''[[rectangle|rectangular]] group'' [2], abstract D<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> or D<sub>4</sub>, also can be represented as a [[direct product]] [ ]×[ ], being the product of two bilateral groups, represents two orthogonal mirrors, with Coxeter diagram, {{CDD|node|2|node}}, with [[Order (group theory)|order]] 4. The '''2''' in [2] comes from linearization of the orthogonal subgraphs in the Coxeter diagram, as {{CDD|node|2x|node}} with explicit branch order 2. The ''rhombic group'', [2]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2}}), half of the rectangular group, the [[point reflection]] symmetry, Z<sub>2</sub>, order 2.

Coxeter notation to allow a '''1''' place-holder for lower rank groups, so [1] is the same as [ ], and [1<sup>+</sup>] or [1]<sup>+</sup> is the same as [ ]<sup>+</sup> and Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_h2}}.

The ''full p-gonal group'' [p], abstract ''[[dihedral group]]'' D<sub>2''p''</sub>, ([[Nonabelian group|nonabelian]] for p>2), of [[Order (group theory)|order]] 2''p'', is generated by two mirrors at angle ''π''/''p'', represented by Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node|p|node}}. The ''p-gonal'' subgroup [p]<sup>+</sup>, ''[[cyclic group]]'' ''Z''<sub>''p''</sub>, of order ''p'', generated by a rotation angle of&nbsp;''&pi;''/''p''.

Coxeter notation uses double-bracketing to represent an [[automorphism|automorphic]] ''doubling'' of symmetry by adding a bisecting mirror to the [[fundamental domain]]. For example, <nowiki>[[p]]</nowiki> adds a bisecting mirror to [p], and is isomorphic to [2p].

In the limit, going down to one dimension, the ''full [[apeirogon]]al group'' is obtained when the angle goes to zero, so [∞], abstractly the [[infinite dihedral group]] D<sub>∞</sub>, represents two parallel mirrors and has a Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node|infin|node}}. The ''[[One-dimensional symmetry group#Translational symmetry|apeirogonal group]]'' [∞]<sup>+</sup>, {{CDD|node_h2|infin|node_h2}}, abstractly the infinite [[cyclic group]] Z<sub>∞</sub>, [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the ''additive group'' of the [[integers]], is generated by a single nonzero translation.

In the hyperbolic plane, there is a ''full [[pseudogon]]al group'' [''iπ/λ''], and ''pseudogonal subgroup'' [''iπ/λ'']<sup>+</sup>, {{CDD|node_h2|ultra|node_h2}}. These groups exist in regular infinite-sided polygons, with edge length λ. The mirrors are all orthogonal to a single line.

In three dimensions, the ''full orthorhombic group'' or ''orthorectangular'' [2,2], abstractly Z<sub>2</sub><sup>3</sup>, [[Order (group theory)|order]] 8, represents three orthogonal mirrors, (also represented by Coxeter diagram as three separate dots {{CDD|node|2|node|2|node}}). It can also be represented as a [[direct product]] [ ]×[ ]×[ ], but the [2,2] expression allows subgroups to be defined:

First there is a "semidirect" subgroup, the ''orthorhombic group'', [2,2<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node|2|node_h2|2x|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node|2|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2}}), abstractly Z<sub>2</sub>×''Z''<sub>2</sub>, of order 4.  When the '''+''' superscript is given inside of the brackets, it means reflections generated only from the adjacent mirrors (as defined by the Coxeter diagram, {{CDD|node|2|node|2|node}}) are alternated. In general, the branch orders neighboring the '''+''' node must be even. In this case [2,2<sup>+</sup>] and [2<sup>+</sup>,2] represent two isomorphic subgroups that are geometrically distinct. The other subgroups are the ''pararhombic group'' [2,2]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h2|2x|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2}}), also order 4, and finally the ''[[Point reflection|central group]]'' [2<sup>+</sup>,2<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h4|2x|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h4|3|2c|3|node_h2}}) of order 2.

Next there is the ''full ortho-''p''-gonal group'', [2,p] ({{CDD|node|2|node|p|node}}), abstractly Z<sub>2</sub>×D<sub>2''p''</sub>, of order 4p, representing two mirrors at a [[dihedral angle]] π/''p'', and both are orthogonal to a third mirror. It is also represented by Coxeter diagram as {{CDD|node|p|node|2|node}}.

The direct subgroup is called the para-''p''-gonal group, [2,p]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h2|p|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2|p|node_h2}}), abstractly D<sub>2''p''</sub>, of order 2p, and another subgroup is [2,p<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node|2|node_h2|p|node_h2}}) abstractly Z<sub>2</sub>×''Z''<sub>''p''</sub>, also of order 2p.

The ''full gyro-p-gonal group'', [2<sup>+</sup>,2''p''] ({{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h2|2x|p|node}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h2|2|p|node}}), abstractly D<sub>4''p''</sub>, of order 4''p''. The gyro-''p''-gonal group, [2<sup>+</sup>,2p<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node_h2|2x|node_h4|2x|p|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|2c|3|node_h4|2x|p|node_h2}}), abstractly ''Z''<sub>2''p''</sub>, of order 2''p'' is a subgroup of both [2<sup>+</sup>,2''p''] and [2,2''p''<sup>+</sup>].

The [[polyhedral group]]s are based on the symmetry of [[platonic solid]]s: the [[tetrahedron]], [[octahedron]], [[cube]], [[icosahedron]], and [[dodecahedron]], with [[Schläfli symbol]]s {3,3}, {3,4}, {4,3}, {3,5}, and {5,3} respectively. The Coxeter groups for these are: [3,3] ({{CDD|node|3|node|3|node}}), [3,4] ({{CDD|node|3|node|4|node}}), [3,5] ({{CDD|node|3|node|5|node}}) called full [[tetrahedral symmetry]], [[octahedral symmetry]], and [[icosahedral symmetry]], with orders of 24, 48, and 120.
[[File:Pyritohedral in icosahedral symmetry.png|thumb|[[Pyritohedral symmetry]], [3+,4] is an index 5 subgroup of [[icosahedral symmetry]], [5,3].]]
In all these symmetries, alternate reflections can be removed producing the rotational tetrahedral [3,3]<sup>+</sup>({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}), octahedral [3,4]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|4|node_h2}}), and icosahedral [3,5]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|5|node_h2}}) groups of order 12, 24, and 60. The octahedral group also has a unique index 2 subgroup called the [[pyritohedral symmetry]] group, [3<sup>+</sup>,4] ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|4|node}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|2|4|node}}), of order 12, with a mixture of rotational and reflectional symmetry. Pyritohedral symmetry is also an index 5 subgroup of icosahedral symmetry: {{CDD|node_n0|5|node_n1|3|node_n2}} --> {{CDD|2_n0|node_n1|3_n0|4|node_h2|3_n1|3_n2|node_h2}}, with virtual mirror '''1''' across '''0''', {010}, and 3-fold rotation {12}.

The tetrahedral group, [3,3] ({{CDD|node|3|node|3|node}}), has a doubling {{Brackets|3,3}} (which can be represented by colored nodes {{CDD|node_c1|3|node_c2|3|node_c1}}), mapping the first and last mirrors onto each other, and this produces the [3,4] ({{CDD|node|3|node|4|node}} or {{CDD|node_c2|3|node_c1|4|node}}) group. The subgroup [3,4,1<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node|3|node|2c|4|2c|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node|3|node|4|node_h0}}) is the same as [3,3], and [3<sup>+</sup>,4,1<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|2c|4|2c|node_h2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|4|node_h0}}) is the same as [3,3]<sup>+</sup>.

=== Affine ===
{{Further|List of planar symmetry groups}}

In the Euclidean plane there's 3 fundamental reflective groups generated by 3 mirrors, represented by Coxeter diagrams {{CDD|node|4|node|4|node}}, {{CDD|node|6|node|3|node}}, and {{CDD|node|split1|branch}}, and are given Coxeter notation as [4,4], [6,3], and [(3,3,3)]. The parentheses of the last group imply the diagram cycle, and also has a shorthand notation [3<sup>[3]</sup>].

{{Brackets|4,4}} as a doubling of the [4,4] group produced the same symmetry rotated π/4 from the original set of mirrors.

Direct subgroups of rotational symmetry are: [4,4]<sup>+</sup>, [6,3]<sup>+</sup>, and [(3,3,3)]<sup>+</sup>. [4<sup>+</sup>,4] and [6,3<sup>+</sup>] are semidirect subgroups.

== Complex reflections==
[[File:Rank2_shephard_subgroups3.png|thumb|[[Hasse diagram]] with all subgroup relations on rank 2 Shephard groups.]]
Coxeter notation has been extended to [[Complex vector space|Complex space]], C<sup>n</sup> where nodes are [[unitary reflection]]s of period 2 or greater. Nodes are labeled by an index, assumed to be 2 for ordinary real reflection if suppressed. [[Complex reflection group]]s are called [[Shephard group]]s rather than [[Coxeter group]]s, and can be used to construct [[complex polytope]]s.

In <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math>, a rank 1 Shephard group {{CDD|pnode}}, order ''p'', is represented as <sub>''p''</sub>[ ], [ ]<sub>''p''</sub> or ]<sub>''p''</sub>[. It has a single generator, representing a 2''&pi;''/''p'' radian rotation in the [[Complex plane]]: <math>e^{2\pi i/p}</math>.

Coxeter writes the rank 2 complex group, <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub> represents [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|pnode|3|q|3|rnode}}. The ''p'' and ''r'' should only be suppressed if both are 2, which is the real case [''q'']. The order of a rank 2 group <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub> is <math>g = 8/q(1/p+2/q+1/r-1)^{-2}</math>.<ref>Coxeter, Regular Complex Polytopes, 9.7 Two-generator subgroups reflections. pp. 178–179</ref>

The rank 2 solutions that generate complex polygons are: <sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> (''p'' is 2,3,4,...), <sub>3</sub>[3]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[6]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[4]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>4</sub>[3]<sub>4</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[8]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>4</sub>[6]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>4</sub>[4]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[5]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>5</sub>[3]<sub>5</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[10]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>5</sub>[6]<sub>2</sub>, and <sub>5</sub>[4]<sub>3</sub> with Coxeter diagrams {{CDD|pnode|4|node}}, {{CDD|3node|3|3node}}, {{CDD|3node|6|node}}, {{CDD|3node|4|3node}}, {{CDD|4node|3|4node}}, {{CDD|3node|8|node}}, {{CDD|4node|6|node}}, {{CDD|4node|4|3node}}, {{CDD|3node|5|3node}}, {{CDD|5node|3|5node}}, {{CDD|3node|10|node}}, {{CDD|5node|6|node}}, {{CDD|5node|4|3node}}. 
[[File:Rank2_infinite_shephard_subgroups3.png|thumb|left|Some subgroup relations among infinite Shephard groups]]

Infinite groups are <sub>3</sub>[12]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>4</sub>[8]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>6</sub>[6]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[6]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>6</sub>[4]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>4</sub>[4]<sub>4</sub>, and <sub>6</sub>[3]<sub>6</sub> or {{CDD|3node|12|node}}, {{CDD|4node|8|node}}, {{CDD|6node|6|node}}, {{CDD|3node|6|3node}}, {{CDD|6node|4|3node}}, {{CDD|4node|4|4node}}, {{CDD|6node|3|6node}}.

Index 2 subgroups exists by removing a real reflection: <sub>''p''</sub>[2''q'']<sub>2</sub> → <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''</sub>. Also index ''r'' subgroups exist for 4 branches: <sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>''r''</sub> → <sub>''p''</sub>[''r'']<sub>''p''</sub>.

For the infinite family <sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub>, for any ''p'' = 2, 3, 4,..., there are two subgroups: <sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> → [''p''], index ''p'', while and <sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> → <sub>''p''</sub>[ ]×<sub>''p''</sub>[ ], index 2.
{{Clear}}

== Computation with reflection matrices as symmetry generators ==

A Coxeter group, represented by [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|node_n0|p|node_n1|q|node_n2}}, is given Coxeter notation [p,q] for the branch orders. Each node in the Coxeter diagram represents a mirror, by convention called ρ<sub>i</sub> (and matrix R<sub>i</sub>). The ''generators'' of this group [p,q] are reflections: ρ<sub>0</sub>, ρ<sub>1</sub>, and ρ<sub>2</sub>. Rotational subsymmetry is given as products of reflections: By convention, σ<sub>0,1</sub> (and matrix S<sub>0,1</sub>) = ρ<sub>0</sub>ρ<sub>1</sub> represents a rotation of angle π/p, and σ<sub>1,2</sub> = ρ<sub>1</sub>ρ<sub>2</sub> is a rotation of angle π/q, and σ<sub>0,2</sub> = ρ<sub>0</sub>ρ<sub>2</sub> represents a rotation of angle π/2.

[p,q]<sup>+</sup>, {{CDD|node_h2|3_n0|3_n1|p|node_h2|3|q|3_n1|3_n2|node_h2}}, is an index 2 subgroup represented by two rotation generators, each a products of two reflections: σ<sub>0,1</sub>, σ<sub>1,2</sub>, and representing rotations of π/''p'', and π/''q'' angles respectively.

With one even branch, [''p''<sup>+</sup>,2''q''], {{CDD|node_h2|3_n0|3_n1|p|node_h2|2x|q|node_n2}} or {{CDD|node_h2|3_n0|3_n1|p|node_h2|2c|2x|q|node_n2}}, is another subgroup of index 2, represented by rotation generator σ<sub>0,1</sub>, and reflectional ρ<sub>2</sub>.

With even branches, [2''p''<sup>+</sup>,2''q''<sup>+</sup>], {{CDD|node_h2|3_n0|3_n1|3_n2|2x|p|node_h4|2x|q|node_h2}}, is a subgroup of index 4 with two generators, constructed as a product of all three reflection matrices: By convention as: ψ<sub>0,1,2</sub> and ψ<sub>1,2,0</sub>, which are [[rotary reflection]]s, representing a reflection and rotation or reflection.

In the case of affine Coxeter groups like {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|4|node_n2}}, or {{CDD|node_n0|infin|node_n1}}, one mirror, usually the last, is translated off the origin. A [[Translation (geometry)|translation]] generator τ<sub>0,1</sub> (and matrix T<sub>0,1</sub>) is constructed as the product of two (or an even number of) reflections, including the affine reflection. A [[transreflection]] (reflection plus a translation) can be the product of an odd number of reflections φ<sub>0,1,2</sub> (and matrix V<sub>0,1,2</sub>), like the index 4 subgroup {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|4|node_n2}}: [4<sup>+</sup>,4<sup>+</sup>] = {{CDD|node_h2|3_n0|3_n1|3_n2|4|node_h4|4|node_h2}}.

Another composite generator, by convention as ζ (and matrix Z), represents the [[Inversion in a point|inversion]], mapping a point to its inverse. For [4,3] and [5,3], ζ = (ρ<sub>0</sub>ρ<sub>1</sub>ρ<sub>2</sub>)<sup>h/2</sup>, where ''h'' is 6 and 10 respectively, the [[Coxeter number]] for each family. For 3D Coxeter group [p,q] ({{CDD|node|p|node|q|node}}), this subgroup is a rotary reflection [2<sup>+</sup>,h<sup>+</sup>].

Coxeter groups are categorized by their rank, being the number of nodes in its [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]]. The structure of the groups are also given with their abstract group types: In this article, the abstract [[dihedral group]]s are represented as ''Dih''<sub>n</sub>, and [[cyclic group]]s are represented by ''Z''<sub>n</sub>, with ''Dih''<sub>1</sub>=''Z''<sub>2</sub>.

=== Rank 3 ===
The finite rank 3 Coxeter groups are [1,''p''], [2,''p''], [3,3], [3,4], and [3,5].

To reflect a point through a plane <math>ax + by + cz = 0</math> (which goes through the origin), one can use <math>\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I} - 2\mathbf{NN}^T </math>, where <math>\mathbf{I}</math> is the 3×3 identity matrix and <math>\mathbf{N}</math> is the three-dimensional [[unit vector]] for the vector normal of the plane.  If the [[L2 norm]] of <math>a, b,</math> and <math>c</math> is unity, the transformation matrix can be expressed as:

:<math>\mathbf{A} = \left [\begin{smallmatrix} 1 - 2 a^2  & - 2 a b & - 2 a c \\ - 2 a b  & 1 - 2 b^2 & - 2 b c  \\ - 2 a c & - 2 b c & 1 - 2c^2 \end{smallmatrix}\right ]</math>

==== [''p'',2] ====
[[File:Spherical decagonal bipyramid.svg|thumb|Example fundamental domains, [5,2], as spherical triangles]]
The reducible 3-dimensional finite reflective group is [[dihedral symmetry]], [''p'',2], order 4''p'', {{CDD|node_n0|p|node_n1|2|node_n2}}. The reflection generators are matrices R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity. [''p'',2]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|p|node_h2|2x|node_h2}}) is generated by 2 of 3 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, and S<sub>0,2</sub>. An order ''p'' [[rotoreflection]] is generated by V<sub>0,1,2</sub>, the product of all 3 reflections.

==== [3,3] ====
[[File:Sphere symmetry group td.svg|thumb|reflection lines for [3,3] = {{CDD|node_c1|3|node_c1|3|node_c1}}]]
The simplest irreducible 3-dimensional finite reflective group is [[tetrahedral symmetry]], [3,3], order 24, {{CDD|node_n0|3|node_n1|3|node_n2}}. The reflection generators, from a D<sub>3</sub>=A<sub>3</sub> construction, are matrices R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity. [3,3]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by 2 of 3 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, and S<sub>0,2</sub>. A [[#trionic subgroup|trionic subgroup]], isomorphic to [2<sup>+</sup>,4], order 8, is generated by S<sub>0,2</sub> and R<sub>1</sub>. An order 4 [[rotoreflection]] is generated by V<sub>0,1,2</sub>, the product of all 3 reflections.

==== [4,3] ====
[[File:Sphere symmetry group oh.svg|thumb|Reflection lines for [4,3] = {{CDD|node_c2|4|node_c1|3|node_c1}}]]
Another irreducible 3-dimensional finite reflective group is [[octahedral symmetry]], [4,3], order 48, {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|3|node_n2}}. The reflection generators matrices are R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>4</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity. Chiral octahedral symmetry, [4,3]<sup>+</sup>, ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by 2 of 3 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, and S<sub>0,2</sub>. [[Pyritohedral symmetry]] [4,3<sup>+</sup>], ({{CDD|node_n0|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by reflection R<sub>0</sub> and rotation S<sub>1,2</sub>. A 6-fold [[rotoreflection]] is generated by V<sub>0,1,2</sub>, the product of all 3 reflections.

==== [5,3] ====
[[File:Sphere symmetry group ih.svg|thumb|Reflection lines for [5,3] = {{CDD|node_c2|5|node_c2|3|node_c2}}]]
A final irreducible 3-dimensional finite reflective group is [[icosahedral symmetry]], [5,3], order 120, {{CDD|node_n0|5|node_n1|3|node_n2}}. The reflection generators matrices are R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>5</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity. [5,3]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by 2 of 3 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, and S<sub>0,2</sub>. A 10-fold [[rotoreflection]] is generated by V<sub>0,1,2</sub>, the product of all 3 reflections.

=== Rank 4 ===
{{Further|Point groups in four dimensions}}
There are 4 irreducible [[Coxeter group]]s in 4 dimensions: [3,3,3], [4,3,3], [3<sup>1,1,1</sup>], [3,4,4], [5,3,3], as well as an infinite family of duoprismatic groups [''p'',2,''q''].

===== <nowiki>[[3,3,3]]</nowiki> =====
The extended group <nowiki>[[3,3,3]]</nowiki>, order 240, is doubled by a 2-fold double rotation matrix T, here reversing coordinate order and sign: There are 3 generators {T, R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>}. ==== [4,3,3] ====
A irreducible 4-dimensional finite reflective group is [[hyperoctahedral group]] (or hexadecachoric group (for [[16-cell]]), B<sub>4</sub>=[4,3,3], order 384, {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|3|node_n2|3|node_n3}}. The reflection generators matrices are R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>3</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>4</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>2</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity.

Chiral hyperoctahedral symmetry, [4,3,3]<sup>+</sup>, ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by 3 of 6 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, S<sub>2,3</sub>, S<sub>0,2</sub>, S<sub>1,3</sub>, and S<sub>0,3</sub>. [[Hyperpyritohedral symmetry]] [4,(3,3)<sup>+</sup>], ({{CDD|node_n0|4|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by reflection R<sub>0</sub> and rotations S<sub>1,2</sub> and S<sub>2,3</sub>. An 8-fold [[double rotation]] is generated by W<sub>0,1,2,3</sub>, the product of all 4 reflections.

==== [3,4,3] ====
A irreducible 4-dimensional finite reflective group is [[Icositetrachoric group]] (for [[24-cell]]), F<sub>4</sub>=[3,4,3], order 1152, {{CDD|node_n0|3|node_n1|4|node_n2|3|node_n3}}. The reflection generators matrices are R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>3</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>4</sup>=(R<sub>2</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity.

Chiral icositetrachoric symmetry, [3,4,3]<sup>+</sup>, ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by 3 of 6 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, S<sub>2,3</sub>, S<sub>0,2</sub>, S<sub>1,3</sub>, and S<sub>0,3</sub>. Ionic diminished [3,4,3<sup>+</sup>] group, ({{CDD|node_n0|3|node_n1|4|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by reflection R<sub>0</sub> and rotations S<sub>1,2</sub> and S<sub>2,3</sub>. A 12-fold [[double rotation]] is generated by W<sub>0,1,2,3</sub>, the product of all 4 reflections.

The hyper-icosahedral symmetry, [5,3,3], order 14400, {{CDD|node_n0|5|node_n1|3|node_n2|3|node_n3}}. The reflection generators matrices are R<sub>0</sub>, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub>. R<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>=R<sub>3</sub><sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>5</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>2</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>3</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=(R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup>=Identity. [5,3,3]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2|3|node_h2}}) is generated by 3 rotations: S<sub>0,1</sub> = R<sub>0</sub>×R<sub>1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub> = R<sub>1</sub>×R<sub>2</sub>, S<sub>2,3</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>×R<sub>3</sub>, etc.

=== Affine rank 2 ===
[[Affine transformation#Representation|Affine matrices]] are represented by adding an extra row and column, the last row being zero except last entry 1. The last column represents a translation vector.

==== [∞] ====
The affine group [∞], {{CDD|node_n0|infin|node_n1}}, can be given by two reflection matrices, x=0 and x=1.

=== Affine rank 3 ===

==== [4,4] ====
{{Further|Tetrakis_square_tiling#Symmetry}}

The affine group [4,4], {{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|4|node_n2}}, (p4m), can be given by three reflection matrices, reflections across the x axis (y=0), a diagonal (x=y), and the affine reflection across the line (x=1). [4,4]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h2|4|node_h2}}) (p4) is generated by S<sub>0,1</sub> S<sub>1,2</sub>, and S<sub>0,2</sub>. [4<sup>+</sup>,4<sup>+</sup>] ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h4|4|node_h2}}) (pgg) is generated by 2-fold rotation S<sub>0,2</sub> and [[glide reflection]] (transreflection) V<sub>0,1,2</sub>. [4<sup>+</sup>,4] ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h2|4|node}}) (p4g) is generated by S<sub>0,1</sub> and R<sub>3</sub>. The group [(4,4,2<sup>+</sup>)] ({{CDD|node|split1-44|branch_h2h2|label2}}) (cmm), is generated by 2-fold rotation S<sub>1,3</sub> and reflection R<sub>2</sub>.

=== Affine rank 4 ===
==== [4,3,4] ====
[[File:Eighth_pyramidille_cell.png|160px|thumb|[4,3,4] fundamental domain]]
The affine group is [4,3,4] ({{CDD|node_n0|4|node_n1|3|node_n2|4|node_n3}}), can be given by four reflection matrices. Mirror R<sub>0</sub> can be put on z=0 plane. Mirror R<sub>1</sub> can be put on plane y=z. Mirror R<sub>2</sub> can be put on x=y plane. Mirror R<sub>3</sub> can be put on x=1 plane. [4,3,4]<sup>+</sup> ({{CDD|node_h2|4|node_h2|3|node_h2|4|node_h2}}) is generated by S<sub>0,1</sub>, S<sub>1,2</sub>, and S<sub>2,3</sub>.

===== <nowiki>[[4,3,4]]</nowiki>  =====
The extended group <nowiki>[[4,3,4]]</nowiki> doubles the group order, adding with a 2-fold rotation matrix T, with a fixed axis through points (1,1/2,0) and (1/2,1/2,1/2). The generators are {R<sub>0</sub>,R<sub>1</sub>,T}. R<sub>2</sub> = T×R<sub>1</sub>×T and R<sub>3</sub> = T×R<sub>0</sub>×T.
